title: Plan 9 from Outer Space

evidence.note: A renewal is on record at the US Copyright Office: RE0000279707, filed in 1986 by Wade Williams under the title 'Plan 9 from Outer Space'. Some argue this renewal is invalid, and the film has long circulated as if it were free, but we found no court ruling or Copyright Office decision on it. Whether the renewal is valid is a legal question we cannot verify, so this layer stays undetermined.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System

evidence.note: CCE Third Series, Parts 12-13: Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan–Dec 1957, Vol. 11 No. 1-2 (archive.org identifier catalogofcopyrig3111213li) confirmed as the contemporaneous registration-year volume for this film. The CCE Third Series ended with the 1977 volume; no printed CCE renewal volume covers the 1984–1987 window when this film's renewal would have fallen due under any of the three plausible first-publication years: 1957 (renewal due 1984–1985), 1958 (renewal due 1985–1986; general release July 1958 per Wikipedia; publication date 1958-05-01 per Copyright Office registration PA0000102338 filed 1981 by Reynolds Pictures Inc.), or 1959 (renewal due 1987). The Copyright Office online catalog (see renewal_absence_search entries above) is the authoritative record for that window. The 1959 Motion Pictures CCE (identifier catalogofcopyrig3131213li) was also located for the alternate publication-year scenario.
evidence.source: Internet Archive / Library of Congress Copyright Office

evidence.note: As a sound film whose copyright registration was never validly renewed, the recorded audio track as embodied in the film shares the print layer's public-domain status. However, the individual musical compositions on the soundtrack may carry their own copyright histories independent of the film's registration: a composition that was separately registered and renewed (or that benefits from post-1978 automatic renewal for works first published 1964–1977) can remain protected even when the film's own registration lapsed. Individual composition research is required before licensing specific musical works for new synchronization or commercial release.

No active franchise or character marks for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space' are known to rights researchers, but trademark status remains formally undetermined pending a completed TESS search.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new U.S. copyright: slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration adds can be protected: a newly composed or recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, or other original creative additions. Use archival prints from archive.org rather than ripping a commercially released disc — ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate the DMCA anti-circumvention provision (17 U.S.C. § 1201) even when the underlying film is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Ed Wood wrote and directed this science-fiction horror film, which had a preview screening in 1957 and went into general theatrical release in July 1958, in which extraterrestrials implement 'Plan 9' — the reanimation of the recently dead — to stop humanity from developing a weapon capable of annihilating the universe. Police officers and airline pilot Jeff Trent pursue the walking corpses under alien control. A renewal is on record at the Copyright Office: RE0000279707, filed in 1986 by Wade Williams under the release title. Some argue that renewal is invalid, and the film's long run on late-night TV and budget video made many people treat it as free, but we found no court ruling or Copyright Office decision that settles it. Until one does, treat Plan 9 as possibly still protected and get advice before reusing it.

Colorized versions add new creative work that is protected on its own, whatever the status of the original black-and-white film.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. A renewal is on record (RE0000279707, filed by Wade Williams in 1986). Some argue it is invalid, but we found no ruling that settles it, so the film's status is undetermined. Get advice before reusing footage.
Is the colorized version of Plan 9 public domain too?
No. Colorization adds new creative authorship that is separately protected regardless of the underlying film's status. Use only the original black-and-white version.
